solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: No avoiding unfortunately new cuts in opera (3,8)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: things gone wrong are jumbled out of order
indicatorNotes.cuts in: the N slices into the mix of letters

annotation.surface: An opera-goer grumbles that, sadly, fresh cuts to the production cannot be avoided.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a complaint about an abridged staging, which hides that the answer is the opera itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Don Giovanni is Mozart's opera about the libertine Don Juan.

entries.clue: Alarms papers raised ahead of PM boarding ship (7)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifting a word turns it upwards, so it reads bottom to top
indicatorNotes.boarding: MAY gets on board, inside the ship's letters

annotation.surface: Newspapers stir panic by printing that the Prime Minister has gone aboard a ship.
annotation.walkthrough: PM looks like the time of day but is the Prime Minister; Theresa May led the UK from 2016 to 2019.
annotation.definitionFit: To dismay someone is to alarm them.

entries.clue: Interference in love lives maiden virtually admits (5)

indicatorNotes.virtually: almost all of the word, so its last letter goes
indicatorNotes.admits: the shortened word lets the others in

blocks.note: née (maiden name) minus its last letter
O = love, a zero score in tennis

annotation.surface: Someone meddles in the love life of a young woman who nearly confesses it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maiden' is not the cricket over or a girl but née, the word introducing a woman's maiden name.
annotation.definitionFit: Noise is unwanted interference on a radio or signal.

entries.clue: Bird, one returning to eat Charlie’s salad plant (7)

indicatorNotes.returning: going back, so the letters run the other way
indicatorNotes.to eat: the reversed letters take C inside them

blocks.note: a grebe is a diving water bird
Charlie is the NATO alphabet word for C, so it stands for that letter

annotation.surface: A bird comes back to peck at Charlie's lettuce.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's on Charlie's is just 'is' in the surface; C goes in after the I of IEBERG.
annotation.definitionFit: Iceberg is a crisp variety of lettuce.

entries.clue: Reeves perhaps succeeded restricting debt, being brutal (7)

annotation.definitionNote: 'being brutal' stands for the adjective, as in 'vicious' = 'brutal'

indicatorNotes.restricting: VIC and S hem the debt in between them

blocks.note: S = succeeded, as in family trees
an IOU is a note of debt

annotation.surface: A chancellor imposes harsh limits on borrowing — Rachel Reeves perhaps, though the solver needs another Reeves.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor; the wordplay wants Vic Reeves, a British TV comedian, and 'perhaps' flags that he is one example of a Vic.
annotation.definitionFit: Vicious and brutal both describe savage cruelty.

entries.clue: Major’s wife tells untruths, it’s said to become regular (9)

indicatorNotes.it’s said: spoken rather than written, so the spelling can differ

blocks.note: Norma Major, wife of Prime Minister John Major

annotation.surface: A political wife is accused of lying so often that it becomes routine.
annotation.walkthrough: Major is not an army rank but John Major, UK Prime Minister 1990–97, whose wife is Norma.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the -ize verb built on normal, meaning to settle into the usual pattern.

entries.clue: Crazy singer overlooked by current bank (7)

indicatorNotes.overlooked by: in a down clue, the thing looking over sits above, so IN comes first

annotation.surface: A deranged vocalist is watched over by a river's flow from its bank.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' is not an anagram signal but the title of Patsy Cline's best-known song.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun sense of bank, a sloping rise of ground as beside a river, not the money sense the surface's current suggests.

entries.clue: Difficulty keeping on the move exposed enemy (7)

indicatorNotes.keeping: HOLE holds the other letters inside
indicatorNotes.exposed: stripped of its outer layer, so first and last letters go

blocks.note: first part of HOLE, as in 'in a hole'

annotation.surface: Trouble follows someone who stays on the run from an unmasked foe.
annotation.walkthrough: Astir means up and about; 'exposed' strips its first and last letters, leaving STI.
annotation.definitionFit: Hostile is used as an adjective for the enemy, as in 'hostile forces'.
annotation.definitionNote: enemy is used attributively, as in 'enemy aircraft'

entries.clue: Teacher, you heard, clad in Elizabethan garb married Daisy (11)

indicatorNotes.you heard: the word as spoken gives the single letter U
indicatorNotes.clad in: someone clad in clothes is inside them, so U goes inside the letters of HOSE

blocks.note: hose = the tights worn by Elizabethan men
the letter U sounds like you
an aster is a daisy-like flower

annotation.surface: A man in period costume marries a woman called Daisy.
annotation.walkthrough: Daisy looks like a bride's name but is the flower family; a housemaster runs a boarding house at a British school.
annotation.definitionFit: A housemaster is a teacher in charge of a boarding house.

entries.clue: Motorists like going on about capital city (7)

indicatorNotes.going on: RAC and AS go on after CA

blocks.note: the RAC, the UK's Royal Automobile Club

annotation.surface: Drivers tend to talk endlessly about the capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going on about' reads as one phrase, nagging; here 'going on' places the pieces and 'about' is CA.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Venezuelan capital is one instance of a capital city.

entries.clue: Sister’s upset with what clothing items? (5-6)

indicatorNotes.upset: knocked over, so the letters fall into new order

blocks.note: the 's counts as a letter S

annotation.surface: A nun is upset — and what are these garments?
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s counts in the fodder; 'with' only joins the two parts of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: these long-sleeved cotton tops are one kind of garment, and the plural matches 'items'.

entries.clue: Star detailed flipping time period for treatment … (5)

indicatorNotes.detailed: de-tailed: the tail letter comes off
indicatorNotes.flipping: turned over, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: an age = a period of time

annotation.surface: A star lists in detail a long spell of medical treatment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' seems to mean itemised; read it as de-tailed, with the tail removed.
annotation.definitionFit: Usage means the way something is treated or handled.

entries.clue: … reminiscent of essentially problematic case (9)

indicatorNotes.essentially: at its essence, the core, so the central letter

blocks.note: the vocative is a grammatical case

annotation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: treatment that recalls a difficult medical case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' reads as a patient's case after 10 across, but it is a grammatical case, used to address someone.
annotation.definitionFit: Evocative means reminiscent of something, calling it to mind.

entries.clue: Resultant commotion finally stops European making legal claim (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: what comes finally comes at the end, so only the last letter of commotion is used
indicatorNotes.stops: plugs a gap, so N goes inside

blocks.note: suing = pursuing a claim in court

annotation.surface: The upshot of an uproar is that a European ends up filing a lawsuit.
annotation.walkthrough: N stops the phrase E SUING up, sitting between its first two letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Ensuing means following as a result.

entries.clue: Curse awful rat epidemic I’d eliminated (9)

indicatorNotes.awful: badly made, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.eliminated: something eliminated is got rid of, so the letters I and D are struck out of rat epidemic

annotation.surface: Someone swears about a dreadful plague of rats they have wiped out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'd' is not the speaker but the letters I and D to be taken out of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: To imprecate is to curse, calling down evil on someone.

entries.clue: Gutless sign that is most dishonest (7)

indicatorNotes.Gutless: with the insides removed, leaving only the outer letters

annotation.surface: A cowardly signal is the most deceitful one.
annotation.walkthrough: Snide in older British use means counterfeit or dishonest, not only sneering.
annotation.definitionFit: Snide can mean sham or dishonest, so snidest is most dishonest.

entries.clue: Before work a police officer gulps large drink (7)

indicatorNotes.Before: the police officer comes ahead of the work
indicatorNotes.gulps: what you gulp ends up inside you, so A COP takes L inside it

blocks.note: a cop is a police officer

annotation.surface: A police officer knocks back a big drink before starting a shift.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Large drink' looks like one phrase; large is L and drink alone is the definition. An alcopop is a sweet bottled alcoholic drink.
annotation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a ready-mixed alcoholic drink.

entries.clue: Was slow in ultimately changing England batsman (7)

indicatorNotes.ultimately changing: the final letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: Zak Crawley, England Test opener, minus his last letter Y

annotation.surface: A batsman was slow in adapting his game for England.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue does not say what the new last letter is; the definition in the past tense fixes it as D.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: moving at a snail's pace, as traffic does in a jam.

entries.clue: Move on from Dundee Corporation, heading north (7)

indicatorNotes.from: the letters are taken from within the words
indicatorNotes.heading north: in a down clue, going upwards means reading back

annotation.surface: Someone leaves Dundee council and travels north.
annotation.walkthrough: Dundee is already in Scotland, so 'heading north' sounds like travel; in a down entry it turns the hidden letters upward.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to go forward to the next stage, as in 'proceed to checkout'.

entries.clue: Discover dad’s sister when undressed has heavenly body (7)

indicatorNotes.when undressed: clothes off: the outer letters are stripped

annotation.surface: Finding a naked aunt with a divine figure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' invites a joke about the aunt's figure; it is simply a planet.
annotation.definitionFit: Literally digging something out of the ground, used figuratively for finding hidden facts.

entries.clue: Suffer collapse when cycling (7)

indicatorNotes.when cycling: letters are moved round from one end to the other

blocks.note: cycling indicator: GO moves from front to back

annotation.surface: A cyclist takes a fall during a ride.
annotation.walkthrough: Cycling reads as bike riding; here it rotates GO from the front of GO UNDER to the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of enduring something unpleasant, as with surgery or hardship.

entries.clue: Sympathy with criminal charge Left is backing (7)

indicatorNotes.is backing: PORT comes at the back, after RAP

blocks.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in 'take the rap'
port = left side of a ship

annotation.surface: The political Left sympathetically supports someone facing a criminal charge.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a reversal signal or political support; it only places PORT at the back.
annotation.definitionFit: Rapport is sympathy and understanding between people.

entries.clue: Figure from Oz partied wildly (9)

indicatorNotes.wildly: out of control, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A character from the Wizard of Oz had a wild party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Figure' reads as a character in a story; it means a geometric shape.
annotation.definitionFit: A trapezoid is a four-sided geometric figure.

entries.clue: Skip using leg splint, on reflection wrongly removed (5)

indicatorNotes.on reflection: mirrored, so the letters run backwards
indicatorNotes.removed: taken out of the splint's letters

blocks.note: start of CALLIPER, a metal leg brace (British spelling)
ill = wrongly; reversed it is LLI, the letters that come out of CALLIPER

annotation.surface: Someone skips about despite wearing a leg brace that was fitted wrongly.
annotation.walkthrough: The British spelling CALLIPER, with two Ls, is needed for LLI to come out; 'ill' as in 'ill-advised' means wrongly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean leaping about in a light, playful way.

entries.clue: Needing breather after core of reactor gets stuck (5)

indicatorNotes.core of: the centre of a word, its middle letter
indicatorNotes.after: what comes after something follows it, so the breather's letters are written after C

blocks.note: a lung is the organ you breathe with

annotation.surface: After a reactor meltdown, someone gasping for air is trapped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Breather' suggests a rest; here it is the organ that breathes.
annotation.definitionFit: Clung means stuck fast to something.

entries.clue: Free publication (7)

blocks.note: free as a verb: to let go, as with a prisoner
a publication is something issued to the public, like a new record or film

annotation.walkthrough: Free is a verb here, not the price of the publication.
annotation.definitionFit: Release means both to free and a published issue.

entries.clue: Outside American university scour ground to find husky (7)

indicatorNotes.ground: crushed up, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Outside an American college, searching the grounds for a sled dog.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Husky' reads as the sled dog but means hoarse-voiced; 'ground' is past tense of grind.
annotation.definitionFit: A raucous voice is harsh and hoarse, like a husky one.

entries.clue: Learned name adopted by endlessly brave, fearless person (11)

indicatorNotes.adopted by: taken in, so READ N sits inside the other word
indicatorNotes.endlessly: a word without end has lost its final letter, so DOUGHTY drops its Y

blocks.note: first letter of DOUGHT, which comes from DOUGHTY
rest of DOUGHTY minus its last letter

annotation.surface: A scholar's name is taken up by a brave, fearless hero.
annotation.walkthrough: Learned is the adjective (LURN-id), as in well-read; doughty is an old word for brave.
annotation.definitionFit: A dreadnought is literally one who dreads nought, a fearless person.
